# Signal: Lock the One Constraint Worth a Sprint

:::{.callout-important}
## In Brief
Signal is the discipline of refusing to move forward until one constraint has been identified precisely, confirmed against actual numbers, and quantified in dollars or hours. By the time you finish this stage, you've got a one-page Constraint Statement that names the problem, where it lives, how long it has existed, and what it has cost. That dollar number is what every AI Sprint downstream has to earn back.
:::

Jesse was in our own L10, reviewing the scorecard for our project management function. The numbers weren't red, they were blank. Tasks were being created but not updated. Client deliverables were slipping by days without anyone flagging it. Billing was late because nobody could confirm what had been delivered and what hadn't. We were paying a project coordinator $24,000 a year as a subcontractor, and the work was still falling behind.

So we asked the question we ask clients all the time: what is this costing us? Not the subcontractor's invoice. The real number. Billing that went out late. Deliverables that slipped. The hours our VP of Operations burned chasing task updates instead of running operations.

Nobody had it. We'd lived with the problem long enough that it stopped registering as a problem at all. The coordinator was failing, but the role was also inadequate. The work required someone in the system constantly, updating tasks and flagging overdue items. No part-time subcontractor was going to sustain that, and hiring a full-time person meant $50,000 or more for work that was largely mechanical.

The real question was whether this was a capacity problem, a capability problem, or whether we could redesign the work itself. That question launched us down the path that became Source and Design.

That conversation was the first time we named the constraint instead of the symptom. The symptom was "tasks are falling behind." The constraint was structural: the project coordination function required constant, systematic attention that no human in the role, at the price point we could justify, was going to sustain. Without Signal, teams reach for a new hire or a workaround, and the constraint stays where it was.

## What Signal produces: one sentence with a dollar number *attached*

Signal produces one artifact: a one-page Constraint Statement `jf-note: a statement isn't one-page. its a sentence.`. Its single anchoring sentence names the problem, where it lives in the org, how long it has existed, and what it has cost in dollars, time, or margin. The rest of the page surrounds that sentence with the evidence that validates it `jf-note: so what? whats the point/context for this?`.

{{< excalidraw ch04-constraint-statement-template "Constraint Statement template: one sentence, location, duration, quantified cost, and validating evidence." >}}

The anchoring sentence follows this structure: "[Function] can't [desired outcome] because [root cause], which costs us [X dollars] per [Y time period]." 

That form names the function that's failing, the outcome that's blocked, and the structural cause rather than the symptom. "Elena can't quote within 24 hours because she's the sole holder of customer pricing context, which costs us approximately $558K per year." That's a constraint you can act on.

You may arrive at this conversation `jf-note: what conversation?` with five candidates `jf-note: 5 candidates for what?`. The job of Signal isn't to delete the other four. You'll always have a backlog. The job is to focus the Sprint: pick the one constraint that, if removed, would change the math most `jf-note: this is an awkward sentence. i dont know what we mean...if we were to do a pilot, would it move the math the most? math is what? cost? time? what about probability of success? The point is that all sprints must be constrained. Ordering the constraints for the purpose of focus is a different exercise. that's more like organizing the backlog. the point is to be clear about what the sprint is focused on. ordeirng the backlog and committting to a focused project are two different things.`, and commit to it for the length of the Sprint.

That commitment is structural. A Sprint that tries to solve three problems solves none of them. A Sprint that solves one produces a measurable result against a number you wrote down at the start, and that result becomes the proof point that earns the next Sprint. The narrowness is what makes the work pay.

The quantified cost is non-negotiable `jf-note: the cost is non-negotiable? or not having one documented?`. A constraint needs a number on it. "The quoting bottleneck is costing us $558K per year in lost revenue, misallocated time, and floor underutilization" is a constraint you can work with. The number tells you whether the constraint is worth a Sprint's attention. It gives the Deliver phase a target to measure against. And it names the opportunity cost. Without it, you can't prove the Sprint paid for itself. `jf-note: this all reads like AI`

:::{.callout-tip}
## Pro Tip
"Significant" isn't a number. Neither is "a lot." Hours per week, dollars per quarter, margin lost, deals not closed — pick a unit and estimate it.
:::

Signal is a gate. You don't move to Source until the constraint is locked: one validated Constraint Statement, in writing, with a number on it and everyone in the room agreeing it names the right problem. If you run EOS, think of Signal as a deeper, root-cause version of IDS — the Issues list traced all the way to the structural constraint underneath, not just named and tabled.

The most common reason teams can't lock the gate is political, not technical. The leadership team can't agree on which constraint is the constraint, so they punt. They pick three, or they write something so abstract nobody can act on it. If your team can't pick one, you've learned something important before a single line of the Sprint has been built: the leadership team is unclear about its priorities.

Julie has watched this discipline land outside any AI context. In a post-acquisition integration at a global food safety company, the presenting problem was a talent gap. Leadership teams in the acquired division were underperforming, and the business instinct was to replace several key leaders.

Before any replacement decision, Julie ran the equivalent of Signal. What was the actual constraint, where did it live, what was it costing? Tracing the underperformance to its root revealed it concentrated in roles where two reporting lines crossed: matrix structures inherited from the Fortune 500 parent, with no clear decision authority assigned. The leaders were operating inside a structure that made it impossible to perform. The constraint was how authority was assigned, not who held the seats. Replacing them would have cost more and fixed nothing: months to hire and ramp new leaders who would have hit the same wall. No one was replaced. The redesign closed the gap.

## Trace the symptom until you reach *structure*

Quoting takes too long because three different systems hold pieces of the customer record, and the ops manager is the only person who knows how to reconcile them. Onboarding is messy because the handoff between sales and delivery is undefined, and every new customer triggers a custom escalation chain. The symptom is what the team feels. The constraint is the structure underneath that produces the feeling.

The same distinction holds in human-capital work. "Our managers aren't developing their people" is a symptom leadership teams treat as a personnel problem for years. The constraint underneath might be that managers have no time for development conversations because their operational workload has grown to absorb every hour. Or it might be that the performance system creates no accountability for development outcomes, so the conversations never happen because nothing bad happens when they don't. Treat the symptom and the cost stays on the books.

{{< excalidraw ch04-symptom-to-constraint "Symptom to constraint: three complaints traced from the visible symptom to the structural cause and what it costs." >}}

A few patterns reliably surface the constraint underneath the symptom. These are the first places to look, not an exhaustive list:

**Conversations that keep coming up but never get resolved.** If your team has been discussing the same issue for two quarters and nobody has fixed it, the issue is a symptom. The constraint is whatever makes it unresolvable. Ask what would have to change structurally for this conversation to stop recurring.

**Workarounds.** Every manual process that exists because something upstream failed is a constraint. The workaround tells you the symptom was visible enough that someone built a patch for it. The patch points directly at the structural failure underneath.

**Sausage-making.** Every organization has processes nobody would want a customer, a board member, or a new hire to watch. The discomfort you feel imagining that observation is pointing at the constraint. Name it.

**Turnover.** When the same role keeps bouncing people out, the role is the symptom. The constraint is the structural failure the role was built on top of. Nobody can succeed in a role where the work was never designed to succeed.

**New-hire confusion.** What does a new person always find confusing in their first ninety days? Where they stumble is where the work is implicit, undocumented, or contradictory, and that's where a constraint hides.

### A PT clinic that almost opened a *sixth location*

Julie sat in on a meeting with a PT clinic operator that was forty-five minutes into a conversation about opening their sixth location. Site selection, lease terms, staffing — everyone around the table owned a piece of the vision.

Julie asked what their clinical efficiency rating was across the five clinics they already had. The room went quiet. Nobody knew. Julie walked to the whiteboard, drew the formula, and they worked the numbers together. The number came out between 58 and 63 percent depending on the location. Industry standard for expansion is 83.

{{< excalidraw ch04-efficiency-gap "Clinical efficiency gap: actual 58–63% vs. expansion threshold of 83%." >}}

Julie put the marker down and said: we've spent four hours today discussing a sixth facility, and the five you already own are running at 60 percent efficiency. You're not ready to expand. Stop that conversation.

The room agreed. What was the constraint underneath the efficiency gap? Scheduling. When patients canceled, nobody filled the slots fast enough. The front desk ran the replacement loop by hand — checking the waitlist in the EHR, calling patients one by one, hoping someone could come in on short notice. A backlog of people who wanted appointments sat in the system. The process connecting them to the open slots was broken. Thirty-seven to forty-two percent of cancellation slots went unfilled, despite a waitlist of patients who wanted those appointments.

The expansion plan was a symptom. The scheduling loop was the constraint. The gap between 60 and 83 told them which one to work on.

{{< excalidraw ch04-five-whys-chain "The PT clinic traced from the symptom (efficiency 58–63%) down to the structural constraint, the scheduling loop, with the stop rule that keeps you off the people layer." >}}

Here is what their Constraint Statement looked like once they'd traced and quantified it:

| Field | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Constraint** | Patient cancellation slots are filled manually by front desk staff, leaving 37-42% of slots unfilled despite a backlog of patients waiting for appointments. |
| **Where it lives** | Front desk → scheduling workflow → manual process of matching cancellations to the waitlist. All 5 locations. |
| **Duration** | ~2 years (since third location opened). Workaround normalized — staff treats manual slot-filling as their job, not as a broken process. |
| **Quantified cost** | Efficiency at 58-63% vs. 83% expansion threshold. ~$420K/year in unrealized revenue (22 unfilled slots/week × $75 avg visit × 5 locations × 50 weeks). Blocking planned 6th location — est. $200K+ in delayed expansion revenue. |
| **Validating evidence** | Efficiency calculated live in leadership meeting. Front desk confirmed manual process. Waitlist exists in EHR but not connected to cancellation notifications. No staff member disputed the gap. |

Anybody in that company could read it and understand what the Sprint was solving without asking a follow-up question.

## Run *Signal* yourself

Signal is a facilitated conversation with your leadership team, not a solo exercise. The rest of this section walks the session step by step, with Meridian Manufacturing (the fictional manufacturer we've been following) as the worked example.

There's no time budget on this. The session runs until the Constraint Statement is written.

{{< excalidraw ch04-constraint-path "The path Signal walks: surface the candidates, trace each to root, confirm the load-bearing one, quantify the cost, and lock a single constraint on paper." >}}

<!-- moves:run-signal-session -->
### How to run the *Signal* session

1. **Assemble the room.** Get the CEO, senior leadership, the owner of the function the constraint sits inside, and a facilitator in one place. The constraint has to be validated by the people who own the business.
2. **Surface the candidates.** Run the lenses from the section above as live questions and write down everything that's broken or slow — no filtering, no debate. Aim for at least five to ten candidates.
3. **Trace each to root with the Five Whys.** Most candidates are symptoms. Keep asking why until the answer lands on a workflow, a handoff, or a structural gap, not a person. `jf-note: shouldn't there be some sort of sorting function first? where do we rank and evaluate the opportunity costs? Is this process syllogistcally sound?`
4. **Pick among the survivors.** When more than one candidate survives the trace, apply the tiebreaker rubric in order: foundation first, highest pain in reach, smallest gap, owner in the room, two-quarter horizon.
5. **Quantify and write the Constraint Statement.** Fill in the one-page template — anchoring sentence, location, duration, quantified cost, validating evidence. The cost must be a real number.
6. **Lock it.** Apply the lever test and the restate test, read the statement back, and confirm the room agrees.
7. **Check the failure modes.** Run the seven-item checklist before you hand off to Source.
<!-- /moves:run-signal-session -->

### Assemble the *room*

The room is your senior leadership team (Sales, Operations, Finance) plus whoever runs the function the constraint sits inside. The CEO is in the room. The facilitator can be the CEO, a coach, or a designated lead. The constraint gets validated by the people who own the business, which is why a solo exercise doesn't count.

### Surface the *candidates*

Before you can pick one constraint, you need an honest inventory of what's broken or slow. Run the lenses from the section above as live questions:

1. What are we working around? What manual process exists because something upstream failed?
2. What does a new person always find confusing in their first ninety days?
3. What process would we never let a customer watch?
4. Where do we keep losing the same person or role?
5. What conversation keeps coming up in meetings but never gets resolved?

Write everything down without filtering. Aim for five to ten candidates. Fewer than three and you haven't been honest enough. More than fifteen and you're listing symptoms — group them. Capture them in a simple Issue Surfacer worksheet, tagging each with the pattern it came from so the clusters show:

| # | Candidate (what's broken or slow) | Pattern (recurring / workaround / sausage / turnover) | Owner |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 |  |  |  |
| 2 |  |  |  |
| 3 |  |  |  |
| … |  |  |  |

If you run EOS, Scaling Up, or a similar cadence-based system, most of this inventory is already on the board. The **Issues list** is the obvious input — every L10 and quarterly review produces one, and most items on it are symptoms, but a few traced honestly are constraints. **Stalled rocks** are the second: a rock carried for three quarters without progress is almost always sitting on top of a constraint nobody named. **The headcount conversation** is the third: every time the org reaches for a hire, a constraint is usually hiding under the work that's stretching the team. You don't have to generate candidates from scratch. You have to know where to look, then trace what you find.

Here's how Meridian's team populated the worksheet at the start of their session:

| # | Candidate (what's broken or slow) | Pattern (recurring / workaround / sausage / turnover) | Owner |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Every quote passes through Elena — 3–5 day turnaround vs. 24-hr standard | Recurring (surfaced every L10 for 6+ months) | Elena / Ops |
| 2 | Job costing is reconciled manually after close — nobody knows margin in real time | Workaround (spreadsheet built when ERP reports proved unreliable) | Finance |
| 3 | Workflow visibility: tasks created in PM system but never updated | Recurring + workaround (VP of Ops chases updates by phone) | VP of Ops |

That's the artifact after the surface pass — no filtering, no debate. Three candidates on the board, ready to trace.

:::{.callout-note}
## Action Step
Open a whiteboard or shared doc. List candidates using the five questions above. No filtering, no debate about whether something belongs. Write everything down.
:::

### Trace each to root with the *Five Whys*

Most of what you surfaced is symptoms. The way down to the constraint underneath is a conversation, not a worksheet `jf-note: this sentence doesnt make sense. its both. the point is to drill down`. Take one candidate and keep asking why until the answer stops moving. This tool is the Five Whys, and you run it out loud with the room `jf-note: this is an awkward construction`:

1. Why is this happening? The first answer is almost always another symptom.
2. Why is that the case? Closer.
3. Why does that happen? Now you're near the structure.
4. What's underneath that? The structural cause.
5. What's the root? The constraint itself.

Run it as a back-and-forth, not a form one person fills out alone `jf-note: we are belaboring this point`. Two people rarely trace the same symptom to the same place. The CEO names one cause, the manager closest to the work names another, and the gap between their answers is usually where the constraint is hiding. Keep going until the room lands in the same spot.

**The stop rule.** You've reached the constraint when the answer points to a workflow, a handoff, a missing system, or a structural gap. You haven't reached it when the answer is a person's name or a market condition. If the honest answer to your last "why" is a name ("because Sarah is the only one who knows"), go one layer down. The constraint isn't Sarah. It's that critical knowledge lives in one head with no system to distribute it. The structure put Sarah in that position, and the structure is what a Sprint can fix. The same logic holds for "the wrong person is in the seat": replacing the person rarely fixes the problem because the role was built on a structural gap that breaks whoever sits in it. Push past the person to the structure.

:::{.callout-tip}
## Pro Tip
Issue and constraint identification is hard work. Mark O'Donnell's *Issues!* is an excellent field guide to it.
:::

:::{.callout-note}
## Action Step
Take your top three candidates. Trace each one to root with the Five Whys, out loud, with the people closest to the work in the room. Cross off anything that bottoms out at a market condition, a personality, or a problem you can't put a number on.
:::

When Meridian traced their three candidates, two of them (the workflow-visibility gap and the manual job costing) bottomed out fast. But the quoting bottleneck kept going. Quotes are slow because every one passes through Elena. They pass through Elena because she's the only one who holds customer pricing, material lead-times, and job history together. That knowledge lives only in her head because no system was ever built to distribute it. The root wasn't Elena. It was that the quoting workflow depended entirely on one person's undocumented context. Three candidates survived the trace, ready for the tiebreaker.

### Pick among the *survivors*

```jf-note:
conceptually a good section, but it needs examples. its not intuitive to me that 5 whys would have multiple "survivors"....what do we mean by "survivors" anyways? are survivors constraints? or are they symptoms?
```

When the Five Whys leaves more than one candidate standing, pain level alone won't tell you which to attack first. You need a tiebreaker. Apply this rubric in order; the first candidate that passes all five is where you start.

1. **Foundation first.** Some candidates unblock the others. The test: if you solved this one, would two or more of the others get easier to evaluate or solve? If yes, it goes first.
2. **Highest pain inside reach.** Of the rest, pick the one closest to the operational pain that brought you to the conversation. Not the most interesting candidate, not the easiest — the one on the workflow that's actually hurting.
3. **Smallest gap to resolution.** When two are tied on pain, pick the one with the shortest distance to a locked constraint: the one that already has partial answers, partial documentation, or a person who knows the workflow. A fast lock builds credibility for the harder work behind it.
4. **Owner in the room.** Don't pick a candidate nobody on the leadership team owns. If you can't name the person who'll move it, you've picked a wish, not a constraint.
5. **Two-quarter horizon.** Pick the candidate you can plausibly lock and Sprint inside two quarters with the team you've got. Name the deliverable and the team that ships it. If you can't see it landing, the work is too big and needs to be broken into a tighter constraint first.

For Meridian, the quoting bottleneck cleared all five. Until the leadership team agreed it was *the* constraint, the workflow-visibility and cost-tracking candidates were being measured against a moving target. It carried the clearest pain, had an obvious owner in Elena, and fit a two-quarter horizon. So Meridian's starting point was set: lock the quoting bottleneck as the constraint, then map the workflow around it. Those two moves set up the work in Source and Design.

:::{.callout-tip}
## Pro Tip
When the tiebreaker doesn't produce a clear winner (two candidates pass all five), go with the one whose cost estimate is harder to dispute. The number that survives scrutiny is the one the room will hold each other to.
:::

### Quantify it and write the *Constraint Statement*

Now you write it down. The one-page Constraint Statement is the deliverable:

| Field | Your constraint |
|---|---|
| **Constraint** _(the one anchoring sentence)_ |  |
| **Where it lives** _(function, workflow, locations)_ |  |
| **Duration** _(how long has it been this way)_ |  |
| **Quantified cost** _(dollars, hours, throughput per period)_ |  |
| **Validating evidence** _(who confirmed it, with what data)_ |  |

Work the fields in order. The anchoring sentence forces precision: "[Function] can't [outcome] because [root cause], which costs [X] per [Y]." **Where it lives** names the team, the workflow, and the handoff — if it crosses departments, name the boundary where the breakdown occurs. **Duration** tells you how deeply the workarounds are embedded; anything over twelve months has almost certainly been normalized. **Quantified cost** is the gate. It must be a number.

If the data isn't clean, estimate:

- **Hours:** hours per week the person or team spends on this, times hourly loaded cost, times 52 weeks.
- **Deals:** quotes or opportunities lost or not pursued because of this, times average deal value.
- **Margin:** the margin this line would carry if the constraint didn't exist, minus current margin.
- **Speed:** days this adds to your cycle, times cost of delay per day.

**Validating evidence** records who confirmed the constraint and with what data, so the number isn't one person's guess.

Here's how Meridian filled it in for the quoting bottleneck:

| Field | Meridian's answer |
|---|---|
| **Constraint** | The VP of Operations is the sole bottleneck for quoting — every quote requires Elena's direct involvement, producing 3–5 day turnaround versus a 24–48 hour standard. |
| **Where it lives** | Operations → the quoting workflow, where customer pricing, material lead-times, and job history converge on one person. |
| **Duration** | Long enough to surface in every L10 without resolving — 6+ months named, years in practice. |
| **Quantified cost** | $558K per year in lost revenue, misallocated time, and floor capacity billed against but unused. |
| **Validating evidence** | Surfaced in every L10. Finance confirmed the floor-utilization gap. Elena confirmed she touches every quote. No one in the room disputed the turnaround numbers. |

:::{.callout-tip}
## Pro Tip
The cost field is where Signal lives or dies. If the data isn't clean, don't stall — use the four estimation formulas above to put a defensible number on it.
:::

### Lock *it*

Two tests confirm you're at the root constraint and not still holding a symptom.

**The lever test.** Look at your candidate list and ask: "If we solved this one, how many of the others get easier or go away on their own?" A root constraint is load-bearing. Solving it moves multiple problems. If the answer is "none," you're likely holding a symptom. If the answer is "several," you've found the right one.

**The restate test.** Say it out loud: "All of these problems stem from [your candidate]. This is the problem we need to solve." If the room resists and people reach for other causes, you don't have the root yet. Keep asking why. If the room agrees, you're there.

Read the completed statement back. Ask: "Is this the thing?" If anyone hesitates, you're not locked. Keep refining until the room actually agrees — the kind of agreement where people nod because the math convinced them, not because the meeting has run long.

:::{.callout-note}
## Action Step
Fill in the one-page Constraint Statement template for your chosen constraint. Read it aloud to the team. If the room can't agree this is the one constraint worth a Sprint, you're not done. Keep working until you've got real agreement.
:::

### Check the *failure modes*

Before you call Signal complete, run this checklist:

- **Too abstract.** "We need better processes" isn't a constraint. Can you point to a specific workflow?
- **Too many.** You wrote down three constraints. Pick one.
- **No number.** The cost field is empty or says "significant." Go back and quantify it.
- **Dominant personality resolved the ambiguity.** The most senior person named the symptom first, everyone nodded, and the meeting moved on. The structural cause never surfaced. This is the most common Signal failure in well-run leadership teams. Ask: "Did we pick this because the data points here, or because the first person to speak named it?"
- **Named the person instead of the structure.** "The constraint is Susie" is never the answer. Susie operates inside a structure. If Susie is failing, the structure failed first. This isn't a defense of poor performance. It's a discipline that keeps Signal from becoming a performance review.
- **Solved the symptom.** Your constraint sentence describes what you feel, not what causes it. Run the Five Whys one more time.
- **Can't be solved by a Sprint.** "Our market is shrinking" or "our founder won't delegate" are real, but they're upstream of this book. Signal is for operational constraints a Sprint can address.

If any of these are true, go back. The gate is real. Passing through it with a bad Constraint Statement costs more than the time it takes to fix it.

## Activity is not *Signal*

Skipping Signal doesn't look like failure. It looks like activity: tools being evaluated, demos on Fridays, somebody prompting in Slack. None of it is Signal. The org hasn't named a single constraint it's committed to solving, so the work has nothing to earn back against.

## Put the Constraint Statement on the *Canvas*

```jf-note:
we need an excalidraw, zoomed in, of the statement on the canvas, so its visual
```

The locked Constraint Statement is the first thing written on your Sprint Planning Canvas. It fills the Constraint row at the top of the page and seeds the first row of the Sequence — the constraint every later stage works against.

From there, the Sprint Lead carries it into Source. Source opens with the dollar number already written down and uses it to decide what knowledge and data the Sprint will need. Which records describe the constraint. Who holds the context that isn't written anywhere. What the team has to capture before it can build against the number you just locked.

:::{.callout-note}
## Action Step
Schedule the Signal session. Send one calendar invite and attach the Constraint Statement template. Write your top three candidate constraints in the invite body. The session is locked when a single Constraint Statement is read aloud and the room agrees.
:::

## Reflect on your operation

1. Run the surfacing lenses on your company right now: what process would you never let a customer watch? Where does your team keep losing the same role? What conversation keeps coming up in your L10s but never gets resolved? Which answer feels most expensive?
2. Take that most-expensive answer and run the Five Whys on it out loud. Does the fifth "why" land on a workflow, a handoff, or a structural gap — or on a person? If it's a person, what system failure put them in the position of being the only one who knows?
3. Put a number on it. Use one of the four estimation formulas — hours, deals, margin, or speed — and write the cost as dollars per quarter or per year. If you can't, you don't have a constraint yet; you have a complaint.
4. If you polled your leadership team individually and asked, "What is the one operational problem AI should solve for us?" — how many different answers would you get? The gap between them is what Signal closes.

Source maps what your company actually knows about the constraint you just locked. The dollar number goes with it.
